title: Spiral review: fluid responsiveness when the tests fail, non-resolving pneumonia, and lactate after valve surgery
description: A Saturday spiral review. Fluid responsiveness and de-resuscitation with the rise and fall of starch and the CHEST trial, community-acquired pneumonia that fails to resolve, and lactate after aortic valve replacement with a worked blood gas. Journal watch on PELICAN, then a round-up of blood gas analysis, ABG interpretation, diabetes insipidus, SIADH and electrolyte replacement.

takeaways: Fluid responsiveness is a 10 to 15 percent rise in stroke volume after fluid; it is not hypovolaemia, so ask three questions: is there hypoperfusion, will fluid help, is fluid safe.

Pulse pressure variation above about 12 percent is valid only when passive, in sinus rhythm, with tidal volume at least 8 mL/kg and a closed chest; otherwise use passive leg raise (cardiac output rise of 10 percent or more) or a 15-second end-expiratory occlusion (rise of 5 percent or more).
CHEST (7,000 patients): starch versus saline, 90-day mortality 18.0 vs 17.0 percent, but renal replacement therapy 7.0 vs 5.8 percent (RR 1.21); SSC 2021 recommends strongly against starches.
VASSPR: starting vasopressin at a noradrenaline-equivalent of 0.1 versus 0.4 mcg/kg/min did not change 28-day mortality (31.8 vs 33.0 percent).

Your CAP fix: structure non-resolving pneumonia as wrong drug, complication, non-infective mimic, or different organism, and list the BAL, antigens, serology, QuantiFERON, vasculitis screen, echo, CT and biopsy.
CAPE COD: hydrocortisone 200 mg/day in severe CAP without shock cut 28-day mortality from 11.9 to 6.2 percent.
Your acid-base fix: Winters' expected PCO2 is 1.5 x HCO3 + 8 plus or minus 2; delta ratio 1 to 2 means pure HAGMA; correct the anion gap for albumin (add 0.25 per g/L below 40).
Your DI fix: free water deficit = 0.6 x weight x (Na/140 - 1), about 8.7 L for a 70 kg man with sodium 169; correct chronic hypernatraemia by no more than 10 mmol/L per day.

title: Deep dive: rhabdomyolysis and crush, the kidney in the line of fire
description: Wednesday deep dive. Rhabdomyolysis and crush injury: where the syndrome came from, the causes the College wants by category, why the kidney fails, the calcium and phosphate traps, and what actually changes outcome. Landmark trials STARRT-AKI and PLUS, then the 2020 first-sitting rhabdomyolysis question read in full and worked by an examiner and candidate.

takeaways: Rhabdomyolysis is a CK more than 5 times the upper limit of normal (usually above about 1,000 U/L). Kidney injury becomes more likely above about 5,000, but CK alone predicts poorly.

For 'list five causes', give five different categories with examples, at 0.5 marks each: crush or immobility, exertion or seizures, ischaemia or compartment syndrome, temperature (heat stroke, NMS, MH), drugs and toxins (statins with fibrates, propofol, cocaine), infection, and metabolic causes (low potassium or phosphate).
AKI has four hits: tubular myoglobin casts in acidic urine, haem-iron oxidative injury, nitric-oxide scavenging causing vasoconstriction, and hypovolaemia from fluid sequestered in muscle.

Crush fluids (ERA field guidance): isotonic saline about 1 L/h, ideally before extrication, 3 to 6 L in the first 6 hours, no potassium-containing fluid in the field. In ICU, titrate to a urine output of 1 to 3 mL/kg/h. Stop escalating if anuric and plan dialysis.

Don't replace early hypocalcaemia unless there's tetany, arrhythmia or hyperkalaemia with ECG changes, because calcium deposits in muscle and rebounds as hypercalcaemia. Hypophosphataemia causes rhabdo; hyperphosphataemia is its consequence.
Bicarbonate and mannitol have no RCT support (Brown 2004: no benefit with CK above 5,000). The College gives no marks either way. Dialysis is for standard indications only, not myoglobin clearance.

PLUS (2022, n=5,037): balanced fluid vs saline, 90-day mortality 21.8% vs 22.0%. STARRT-AKI (2020, n=3,019): accelerated vs standard RRT, mortality 43.9% vs 43.7%, with more dialysis dependence at 90 days (10.4% vs 6.0%).
Your crush question (2025.1 Q3): 4.5/10 on 12 Oct, then 7/10 on 15 Oct. When a stem says 'blood and fluid', give fluid equal weight, with a rate and a target.

title: Shock: classify it by mechanism, prove it with the numbers
description: Consultant tutorial: defining shock, the four mechanisms with the haemodynamic pattern for each, and the limits of bedside perfusion signs in a ventilated patient. Then an examiner and candidate work a cardiogenic versus septic shock data question. Study day Wednesday 28 October.

chapters.title: Exam practice: cardiogenic vs septic shock

takeaways: Shock is inadequate oxygen delivery or use at the cellular level. Hypotension is common but not required (ESICM 2014 consensus).

Classify by mechanism: hypovolaemic, cardiogenic, obstructive, distributive (plus cytotoxic). Mixed shock is common. In SOAP II, about 62% of shocked ICU patients were septic and about 2% obstructive.

Haemodynamic patterns: hypovolaemic = low filling pressures, low output, high SVR, low SvO2. Cardiogenic = wedge high (often >18), CI <2.2 on support, high SVR, low SvO2. Obstructive = low output and high SVR, with pressures set by the site (tamponade equalises diastolic pressures within about 5 mmHg). Distributive = low SVR, normal or high output and SvO2.
SVR = 80 x (MAP - CVP) / CO; normal 800-1200 dyn.s.cm-5. A high SvO2 in sepsis does not exclude tissue hypoxia.
Septic shock (Sepsis-3): vasopressor needed for MAP 65 or more and lactate >2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid; hospital mortality >40%.

Bedside perfusion: CRT >3 s is abnormal. ANDROMEDA-SHOCK: 28-day mortality 34.9% vs 43.4% (P = 0.06). A Pcv-aCO2 gap >6 mmHg suggests low flow. MAP 65 is the default (SEPSISPAM: no mortality difference at 80-85).
Shock on day 2 after an MI: re-infarction, VSD (oxygen step-up), papillary muscle rupture (large v waves), free wall rupture with tamponade.
